Lecturer's note, Monday. During the economics lecture, Hafsa's phone lit up several times on her desk. She turned it face down but kept glancing at it, and her notes went thin. In the break she told me that a friend had sent a voice note of about five minutes and she could not listen with the class still in session. "I don't want to ignore her, but I need the main point," Hafsa said.
I suggested she reply with a short text asking for a two-line summary and a time to talk later. She typed it in the corridor. The reply came: "Sorry! Just asking if you're coming to the trip. Yes/no?" Hafsa laughed with relief.
Bhavna, lecturer

qa.q: How long was the voice note that arrived during the lecture?
qa.a: The voice note was five minutes long.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling as the phone lit up and she kept glancing at it?
qa.a: Hafsa felt pulled two ways: anxious not to ignore her friend, yet unable to listen during class. Her thin notes show how much her attention was split.

qa.q: What did Bhavna suggest that solved Hafsa's problem?
qa.a: Bhavna suggested a short text asking for a two-line summary and a time to talk later. It gave Hafsa the main point without needing to listen in class.

qa.q: Why might the friend have sent such a long voice note?
qa.a: The friend probably found it easier to talk than type and did not realise Hafsa was in a lecture. The real question was only whether Hafsa was coming to the trip.

grounding: A student receives a five-minute voice note during a lecture and cannot listen, and asks for a text summary.

passage:
Thursday, on the 6:15 local. Packed carriage, no seat, one hand on the pole, bag between my feet. Wasim sent a voice note: 5:08 long. I stared at it. No earphones, the train was roaring, and I could not put it on speaker with a hundred people around.
I felt guilty, then a little irritated. What if it was important? What if it was only a story? I could not tell.
At the next station I typed, "On the train, can't listen. Can you text me the main thing?" 🙂 He replied with two lines: the trip was moved to Sunday. That was all. Next time I will ask him to text first.
— Lokesh

qa.q: How long was the voice note Wasim sent to Lokesh?
qa.a: Wasim's voice note was 5:08 long.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling while staring at the voice note on the train?
qa.a: Lokesh felt guilty and a little irritated. The note might have been important, but there was no way to listen in the noise.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that solved the problem, and what does Lokesh plan next?
qa.a: Lokesh typed a short message asking Wasim to text the main thing, and got two lines back. Next time Lokesh will ask Wasim to text first.

qa.q: How might Wasim have seen a five-minute note when sending it?
qa.a: Wasim probably thought a voice note was easy and friendly, without realising Lokesh was on a crowded train. The real message was small: the trip moved to Sunday.

grounding: A student cannot listen to a five-minute voice note on a train and asks for a text summary.

"Tanuja! Did you listen to my voice note?"
"Mridul, it was five minutes long. I was in Organic Chemistry."
"But it was important!"
"Then I needed it in words. I saw the notification, saw five minutes, and panicked that something was wrong. I couldn't play it with Professor Rao right there."
"Oh. Sorry. It was about the group presentation. Who does which slides."
"Okay, so what's the plan?"
"I take slides one to four, you take five to eight, Aisha does the conclusion."
"That's it? That's two lines!"
"I also talked about the canteen samosas."
"Mridul!"
"Fine. Next time, a text summary first, voice note for the samosas."
"Thank you. I like hearing your voice, honestly. Just not in a lecture."
"Noted. Also, the samosas really were good."
Tanuja shook her head and wrote "slides 5–8" in her notebook.

qa.q: Which slides does Tanuja take?
qa.a: Tanuja takes slides five to eight.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling on seeing the five-minute note in the lecture?
qa.a: Tanuja felt anxious and stuck, panicking that something was wrong but unable to play it with Professor Rao right there.

qa.q: What small, kind change did they agree on?
qa.a: Mridul will send a short text summary first and keep voice notes for chatty things like the samosas.

qa.q: How did Mridul see the voice note before this conversation?
qa.a: Mridul thought it was an easy, friendly way to share important news and didn't realise the demand it put on Tanuja's time.

grounding: A student cannot listen to a five-minute voice note in a lecture and asks for a text summary; the sender hadn't realised the demand.

passage:
I'm Himani, and it was a Tuesday on the Virar fast local, packed so tight I couldn't lift my arm properly. My phone buzzed. Rajni. A voice note. Four minutes and fifty-eight seconds.
Rajni never sends voice notes unless something big has happened. I stood there, crushed between a woman with a vegetable basket and the door, with no earphones, imagining everything from a breakup to a family emergency. I couldn't play it. I couldn't type properly either.
Finally I managed: "on train, no earphones, all ok?? can you text the main thing?"
She replied: "yes all ok!! just the internship result. I GOT IT."
I nearly cheered in the compartment. Later that evening I listened to the whole note properly: four minutes of screaming, thanking her mother, and describing the interviewer's cat.
I loved it. I just loved it more at home, sitting down.

qa.q: How long was Rajni's voice note?
qa.a: It was four minutes and fifty-eight seconds.

qa.q: What was Himani worried about on the train?
qa.a: Himani was anxious that something big had gone wrong, imagining everything from a breakup to a family emergency.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who receives a long voice note at a bad time?
qa.a: Send a quick text like Himani did, asking if all is okay and asking for the main point, then listen properly later.

qa.q: How did Rajni likely feel while recording the note?
qa.a: Rajni felt thrilled and excited about getting the internship, wanting to share every detail, without thinking where Himani might be 🎉

grounding: A student on a train cannot listen to a nearly five-minute voice note and asks for a text summary of the main point.

Lab session note, Wednesday
During the second-year titration practical, Pranav's phone buzzed repeatedly on the bench. He checked the screen, winced, and turned it face down. Twice more it buzzed. On a break he showed me, a little embarrassed: three voice notes from his project partner Eshaan, six, five and four minutes long. Pranav said, "I can't listen here, and if I don't reply he'll think I'm ignoring him."
I suggested he text back that he was in lab and ask for a short text of the main point. He did. Eshaan replied within a minute: "Oh sorry! Just need your part of the report by Friday."
Pranav laughed, but looked relieved. Later Eshaan came by the lab door to apologise; he said he hadn't thought about where Pranav might be.
Next step: I will mention in Monday's briefing that phones stay in bags during practicals, and that a short text is kinder in class hours.

qa.q: How long were Eshaan's three voice notes?
qa.a: They were six, five and four minutes long.

qa.q: Why did Pranav wince when he checked his phone?
qa.a: Pranav felt stressed and worried, unable to listen in the lab but afraid Eshaan would think he was ignoring him.

qa.q: What went right after the supervisor's suggestion?
qa.a: Pranav texted that he was in lab and asked for the main point, and Eshaan's short reply solved it in a minute.

qa.q: How did Eshaan see things once he understood?
qa.a: Eshaan felt sorry, realising he hadn't thought about where Pranav might be, and came to apologise in person.

grounding: An adult's note shows a student unable to listen to long voice notes in a lab, and the sender not realising the demand on his time.

Tuesday night, Salma's journal.
Chetan sent a voice note at 9:40 this morning. Five minutes and twelve seconds. I was on the packed local to Dadar with one broken earphone, wedged between a vegetable basket and someone's elbow. Couldn't play it. Then straight into Prof. Iyer's lecture, phone on silent. By lunch a second one arrived, three minutes long. I had an anxious itch all through the practical: what if it's the project deadline? What if something happened at home? Finally listened at six on the platform. It was mostly about his cousin's wedding playlist. Then, at minute four: "Oh, and can you send the lab file by tonight?" I nearly missed it. Not annoyed exactly; he talks the way he thinks. But I texted: "Love your voice notes, but if it's something I need to do, can you put one line in text too? 🙏" He sent back: "lab file, tonight, sorry!"

qa.q: How long was the first voice note?
qa.a: Five minutes and twelve seconds.

qa.q: What was Salma worried about during the practical?
qa.a: Salma felt anxious that the unheard notes might be about the project deadline or trouble at Chetan's home.

qa.q: What did Salma's text ask for, and why does it help?
qa.a: One line in text for anything to act on, so the key point, like the lab file, is not buried at minute four of a note.

qa.q: Why might Chetan not realise his voice notes were hard to listen to?
qa.a: Chetan talks the way he thinks and probably pictures Salma free to listen, not squeezed onto a local train or sitting in a lecture.

grounding: Shows a student who cannot play a long voice note on a train or in a lecture and asks the sender for a short text line as well.
